A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same alt-test research. All pages, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. The original appendix contents can be matched across renumbering; v4 adds a simulation appendix.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of six LLMs across ten datasets, prompting comparisons, bootstrap analyses, and additional results in its appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and adds original synthetic-data simulation results in Appendix C, Figures 4–5.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same alignment scores, advantage probabilities, hypothesis tests, BY correction, and winning-rate decision rule. The adaptations in v3 Appendix C reappear unchanged in v4 Appendix D; revised epsilon recommendations do not alter the procedure.

E1.justification: All ten original datasets and their tasks are retained. v4 Appendix C adds controlled synthetic discrete-annotation scenarios with varying human/LLM reliability and category counts from 2 to 40, a focused extension of evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated LLMs, prompting and ensemble comparisons in Tables 2–3, and embedding-model comparisons in Table 4 are unchanged. The simulations vary annotator quality without introducing another competing method.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces a substantial controlled simulation protocol: sampled class priors, separately controlled human and LLM noise, and datasets containing six synthetic human annotators and 500 instances. Evaluation samples three annotators and 30–200 instances while sweeping noise, category counts, and four epsilon values. Existing benchmark settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds two systematic sensitivity analyses examining how relative annotator reliability and category counts affect sample requirements and test outcomes. Figures 4–5 expose interactions involving noise, ties, and epsilon that the retained real-data sample-size and epsilon analyses did not isolate.

E5.justification: The new simulations report 50 independently generated datasets per condition and 50 bootstrap samples within each dataset, totaling 2,500 combinations per point. They report empirical 90% intervals for advantage probability. The original 100-bootstrap analyses and their uncertainty reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Figures 4–5 add extensive winning-rate, advantage-probability, agreement, and accuracy results; original benchmark values and rankings remain unchanged. For example, Figure 5 reports majority-vote accuracies of 0.84 with two categories and 0.53 with 40 at fixed human noise 0.5 and LLM noise 0.2, alongside easier test passage with more categories.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a formal stochastic annotation model with Dirichlet-distributed class priors and a noise-controlled mixture of the gold label and class prior. The original mathematical definitions of the alt-test, Theorem 1, and its proof remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions and claims: the alt-test, average advantage probability, empirical demonstration, optimal-judge theorem, and feasibility with modest annotation samples. The simulations provide additional support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Section 7 changes the reassurance that weak, noisy annotators are unlikely to let an LLM pass into an explicit acknowledgment that they can. v4 recommends reporting agreement, using epsilon at most 0.1 when reliability is low, and collecting more annotations. Appendix C also adds explanations involving category counts, ties, and reliability-dependent sample requirements.

D1.justification: v4 documents simulation generation and sampling parameters and newly states that simulation code is available in the existing repository. Appendix A explains customization through category counts and expected agreement. Existing model, prompt, and dataset-processing information is retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Section 2 are unchanged. No cited works are added or removed, and the positioning relative to existing agreement measures and statistical approaches is retained.

P1.justification: v4 adds a reporting FAQ, makes targeted revisions to practical guidance and limitations, inserts the simulation appendix, and updates cross-references and one author affiliation. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds substantial visual material: Figure 4 contains a 5-by-5 noise grid, and Figure 5 a 6-by-5 category/noise grid, with curves, confidence bands, and panel statistics. Existing tables and figures retain their content; Figure 3 moves, and the original tangram Figure 4 becomes Figure 6.

improvement.justification: The controlled simulations and reporting guidance improve practical validation, especially by replacing v3's reassuring weak-annotator discussion with an explicit warning and reliability-dependent recommendations. The benefit is limited by a new error on v4 page 20: the 'Stronger LLM requires fewer instances' passage reverses both the noise inequality and the direction through Figure 4, contradicting the definitions and plot. The original method and benchmark evidence remain intact.
